title: The Map Contract: Associative Key-Value Storage
summary: Understand why Map does not extend Collection, the key-to-value association model, uniqueness of keys, and value mutability.
learningObjectives: Understand the formal mathematical definition of the java.util.Map associative abstraction
Analyze why Map does not extend the java.util.Collection root interface

activities.title: Practical Context: DNS Hostname to IP Address Resolution

analogy.headline: Practical Context: DNS Hostname to IP Address Resolution
analogy.story:
Every time you enter a web address like 'learnbyself.dev', your computer does not store all websites in a single sequential list. Instead, the global Domain Name System (DNS) operates as a distributed key-value directory: a unique hostname acts as the key, pointing directly to a specific IP address value.

Hostnames cannot duplicate—there can only be one 'learnbyself.dev'. However, multiple different hostnames can legitimately point to the exact same IP address (values may duplicate). When server migrations happen, the IP value is updated in-place without altering the domain name identity.

This is precisely how an Associative Map operates in software engineering.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A Map stores associative pairs (Key -> Value). Keys are strictly unique; values can duplicate. Queries prioritize finding a value by its key in O(1) time.

activities.title: The Map Architecture: Associative Arrays & Why Map Is Not A Collection

keyTakeaways: A Map<K, V> models an associative array binding unique keys to arbitrary values
Map does NOT extend java.util.Collection because of an interface contract mismatch (single elements vs key-value pairs)
put(key, value) returns the PREVIOUS value associated with the key, or null if the key was new
Keys form a Set (no duplicates); values form a Collection (duplicates allowed)

activities.content:
### Definition of the java.util.Map Interface

The **`java.util.Map<K, V>`** interface is a core member of the Java Collections Framework representing an object that maps keys to values. Formally, a map cannot contain duplicate keys; each key can map to at most one value. It models the mathematical function abstraction:
$$f : K \to V$$

Unlike `List` and `Set`, **`Map` does NOT extend `java.util.Collection`**. This is an intentional architectural design:
* `Collection<E>` represents a container of individual elements with signatures like `add(E element)` and `iterator()`.
* `Map<K, V>` represents pairwise associations requiring two parameters `put(K key, V value)` and cannot produce an `Iterator<E>` directly without specifying whether keys, values, or entries are being traversed.

---

### Core CRUD Operations & The put() Return Contract

When interacting with a Map:
* **`V put(K key, V value)`**: Associates the specified value with the key. If the map previously contained a mapping for the key, the old value is replaced and **returned**. If the key was absent, it returns **`null`**.
* **`V get(Object key)`**: Returns the mapped value, or `null` if no mapping exists.
* **`V getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)`**: Returns the value if present, otherwise returns `defaultValue` without inserting it into the map.
* **`boolean containsKey(Object key)`**: Checks key existence in $O(1)$ average time.
* **`boolean containsValue(Object value)`**: Checks value existence in $O(N)$ linear time (requires full map scan).

---

### Executable Demonstration: User Session Registry

```java
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class MapContractDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, String> sessionStore = new HashMap<>();

        // 1. Insertion: put() returns null for new keys
        String prevAlice = sessionStore.put("user_101", "192.168.1.10");
        System.out.println("First put('user_101') returned: " + prevAlice); // null

        // 2. Duplicate key: replaces value and returns previous mapping!
        String oldAlice = sessionStore.put("user_101", "10.0.0.99");
        System.out.println("Second put('user_101') returned: " + oldAlice);  // 192.168.1.10

        // 3. Different key mapping to duplicate value (valid in Map)
        sessionStore.put("user_102", "10.0.0.99");

        System.out.println("Total mappings: " + sessionStore.size());        // 2
        System.out.println("Current user_101 IP: " + sessionStore.get("user_101")); // 10.0.0.99

        // 4. Safe lookup with default fallback
        String guestIp = sessionStore.getOrDefault("guest_999", "0.0.0.0");
        System.out.println("Guest IP fallback: " + guestIp);                // 0.0.0.0
    }
}
```

**Console Output:**
```text
First put('user_101') returned: null
Second put('user_101') returned: 192.168.1.10
Total mappings: 2
Current user_101 IP: 10.0.0.99
Guest IP fallback: 0.0.0.0
```

---

### Summary of Map Collection Views

| Method | Return Type | Uniqueness Guarantee | Iteration Performance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`map.keySet()`** | `Set<K>` | Strictly Unique | $O(\text{Capacity} + N)$ |
| **`map.values()`** | `Collection<V>` | Duplicates Allowed | $O(\text{Capacity} + N)$ |
| **`map.entrySet()`** | `Set<Map.Entry<K, V>>` | Unique by Key | $O(\text{Capacity} + N)$ |

questions.question: Why does java.util.Map not extend java.util.Collection?
options: Because Map is part of java.lang, not java.util
Because of a structural mismatch: Collection models single elements (add(E)), while Map models key-value pairs (put(K, V))
Because Map was deprecated in Java 5
Because Map is strictly an abstract class
questions.explanation: Collection represents a group of individual items (Collection<E>). Map requires pairs of objects (K, V). Extending Collection would force incompatible methods like add(Object) onto Map.

questions.question: What is the return value of map.put(key, value) when the key is already present in the map?
options: The new value that was just inserted
The previous value that was replaced by this operation (or null if previously mapped to null)
questions.explanation: put() returns the previous value associated with the specified key, allowing callers to inspect what was overwritten.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of map.containsKey(key) versus map.containsValue(value) in a standard HashMap?
options: containsKey is O(1) average; containsValue is O(N) linear scan
containsKey is O(log N); containsValue is O(1)
questions.explanation: Keys are hashed directly to bucket indices in O(1) average time. Values are not indexed by hash; finding a value requires linearly scanning every node across all buckets O(N).

questions.question: What happens if map.get(key) returns null?
options: It guarantees that the key is not in the map
It means either the key is not in the map, OR the key is present and explicitly mapped to the value null
It removes the key from the map
questions.explanation: In a HashMap that allows null values, get() returning null is ambiguous. To distinguish between a missing key and a key mapped to null, invoke map.containsKey(key).

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to rely on map.get(key) != null to verify if a key exists in a HashMap?
questions.answer: HashMap allows null values. If a key exists in the map with a value of null (e.g., map.put('key', null)), `map.get('key')` returns null. A check like `if (map.get(key) != null)` will falsely conclude the key does not exist. The only authoritative way to verify key existence is `map.containsKey(key)`.

questions.question: What is the relationship between map.keySet() and the underlying map?
questions.answer: map.keySet() returns a backed view of the keys in the map, not a copied snapshot. Removing an element from the keySet (via `keySet.remove(k)`) removes the corresponding key-value pair directly from the underlying map! However, attempting to call `keySet.add(k)` throws an UnsupportedOperationException because a key cannot be added without an associated value.

questions.question: How does getOrDefault() improve code readability and performance over traditional containsKey + get checks?
questions.answer: Writing `if (map.containsKey(k)) return map.get(k); else return default;` performs two separate hash bucket lookups: one for containsKey and another for get. In contrast, `map.getOrDefault(k, default)` calculates the hash and traverses the bucket exactly once, cutting CPU lookup instructions in half while eliminating noisy conditional boilerplate.
